hints: Focus on what ethanolic NaOH does to a halogenoalkane, elimination to form an alkene, and what structural feature it needs.
Remember elimination removes HBr, so you need a hydrogen on the carbon next door to the C-Br carbon.
Draw or picture each skeleton and look for the one where the neighbour carbon has no hydrogens left to lose.
walkthrough:
**Recall the elimination rule**

Ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation. It removes H from one carbon and Br from the adjacent carbon to make a C=C double bond.

General rule:
$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CHBr-R' + NaOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{R-CH=CH-R' + NaBr + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Spot the key requirement**

For an alkene to form, there must be at least one hydrogen on a beta-carbon, that is a carbon directly attached to the $\text{C-Br}$ carbon. If the beta-carbon has no H, elimination is impossible.

**Test the structures**

Options A, B and C all have hydrogens on the neighbouring carbons, so they can all lose HBr easily. Only bromodimethylpropane, which is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-CH}_2\text{Br}$ or 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, has its $\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ joined to a carbon with three methyl groups and no hydrogen.

Structure:
$$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-CH}_2\text{Br}$$

**Conclude**

Since there is no beta-hydrogen to remove, no C=C can form. This matches the observation that no alkene is produced.

options.A: Incorrect. 1-bromo-2-methylbutane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{Br}$. The carbon next to $\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ has one hydrogen, so HBr can be eliminated to give an alkene.
options.B: Incorrect. 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. There are hydrogens on the adjacent $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so elimination readily gives mainly 2-methylbut-2-ene.
options.C: Incorrect. 3-bromopentane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Both neighbouring carbons have hydrogens, so elimination gives pent-2-ene.
options.D: Correct. Bromodimethylpropane is 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C-CH}_2\text{Br}$. The $\text{C-Br}$ carbon is attached to a quaternary carbon with no hydrogens, so there is no beta-hydrogen to lose and elimination to an alkene cannot occur.
